analysis.one_liner: Removes the legal shield that protects government officials from lawsuits over constitutional violations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it received no further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone's constitutional rights are violated by a state or local official — most often a police officer — courts currently allow the official to escape personal liability unless the victim can prove the right was 'clearly established' in prior cases. The bill would strip away that defense, letting victims recover damages from the official directly. It did not change criminal liability or department discipline; it only affected civil lawsuits for money damages.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by government officials acting under color of law — for example, victims of police misconduct. They would no longer have to find a nearly identical earlier court case to recover damages, and they could sue the official personally rather than relying on hard-to-win suits against cities.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the federal civil-rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to state that good faith, a reasonable belief the conduct was lawful, or the right not being 'clearly established' are not defenses to a civil action for deprivation of rights [S3].

The bill's findings section states that qualified immunity has severely limited plaintiffs' ability to recover damages under section 1983 and has frustrated Congress's original intent in passing the 1871 civil rights statute [S3].
The bill would apply to lawsuits pending on, or filed after, its enactment, so people with existing cases could benefit too [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Government officials who violate constitutional rights — including police officers — would face personal financial liability, and the insurers and governments that indemnify them would bear more of those costs. Government agencies would also lose a procedural defense that currently ends many lawsuits early.
analysis.who_pays_short: Government officials and the agencies that insure them

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that removing qualified immunity could expose individual officers and officials to personal liability for split-second decisions, and courts have cited the need to protect officials from the burdens of defending suits when the law was unclear. The bill responds by ending the defense entirely, including for officials who reasonably believed their conduct was legal [S3].

Cities, towns, and their insurers would likely pay more in settlements and judgments, and those costs could be passed to local taxpayers; the bill does not include any provision shifting or capping those costs [S3].

The bill would have no effect on criminal prosecution or on firing or disciplining officers — it changes only the availability of civil damages suits, so it would not by itself remove officers from the streets [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people whose rights are violated, the change is significant: the 'clearly established' rule is widely understood to defeat many meritorious cases before they ever reach a jury. The main cost is financial: officials, governments, and their insurers would face more and costlier lawsuits, some filed over genuinely debatable conduct. Whether that cost falls on the officials themselves or is absorbed by indemnification agreements would matter a great deal in practice, and the bill does not address that question directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, with Senators Sanders and Warren, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The Senate Judiciary Committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill, and no further action appears in the full action history for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The bill never received a floor vote in either chamber and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials — including police officers — and the insurers and governments that cover them are better off, because the judicially created defense shielding them from personal liability for constitutional violations remains in place. Victims of rights violations remain unable to recover in many cases where the right was not 'clearly established.'

against.name: Sen. Charles Schumer

against.name: Police unions and law enforcement groups
against.what_they_did: Have publicly campaigned against ending qualified immunity, arguing it protects officers who must make rapid decisions under uncertainty.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Senate Republican sponsored or supported the bill, and no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: Qualified immunity is the doctrine that shields individual officers from personal liability when they violate constitutional rights. The bill would have removed that shield for civil damages suits; its death keeps the protection intact.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Cities and their insurers absorb most civil-rights judgments today, and the bill would have allowed suits against individual officials as well, raising defense and payout costs. Governments that indemnify their workers would have kept paying in most cases, but would lose the early case-ending defense qualified immunity provides.
